props.title: GitHub Actions in one breath
items: Event → workflow → job → runner → step: the whole model
Filters, schedules and buttons decide WHEN a workflow runs
needs builds a graph; a matrix fans jobs out in parallel

Caches, outputs, artifacts carry data; secrets stay masked
Deploy via environments, approvals and OIDC — no stored keys
Around it: PRs, Issues, Projects, Codespaces, Copilot, security
props.closer: Push code. Let the robots do the rest.

captions: Part ten. The rest of GitHub.
Actions is one piece of a much bigger platform.
Let's tour the other features — the ones your
workflows plug into.
At the center is the repository: your code, its
full history, and its branches.
Around it, GitHub groups its features into a few
families.
Collaborate — pull requests and code review.
Plan — Issues, Projects and Discussions.
Build — Codespaces, and Copilot, the AI assistant.
Automate — Actions, which you now know well.

Secure — Dependabot, code scanning and secret
scanning.
And ship — Releases, Packages and Pages.
Let's walk through them.
The heart of collaboration is the pull request.
You create a branch, commit your change, and open
a pull request to merge it into main.

Teammates review the diff line by line. They
comment,
suggest edits, and approve, or request changes.
A code owners file can require review from the
right team automatically.
Meanwhile, Actions runs the checks.

Rulesets and branch protection enforce the policy —
reviews
required, checks green. And a merge queue can test
changes together before they land.
Then you merge: squash, rebase, or a merge commit.
For planning, there are Issues. Each one tracks a
bug, a task or an idea, with labels, assignees,
and sub-issues for breaking big work down.
Projects turns issues into a planning board — a
table, a kanban board, or a roadmap timeline, with
custom fields like priority and sprint.
Write closes, then the issue number, in a pull

request, and merging it closes the issue
automatically.

For open-ended conversation there's Discussions —
questions, ideas and
announcements, away from the bug tracker.
And a wiki, for longer documentation.

Codespaces gives you a full development environment
in the
cloud.

Click Code, then create codespace, and in seconds
you're
in VS Code — in your browser or on
your desktop — on a cloud machine with your
repo already cloned.
A dev container file defines the tools, so every

contributor gets an identical setup. No more setup
documents.

Personal accounts get a free monthly allowance of
core
hours.

It's perfect for onboarding, reviewing a pull
request properly,
or coding from a tablet.
Then there's Copilot, GitHub's AI assistant.
In your editor, it completes code as you type,
and answers questions in chat.
On github dot com, it can review pull requests
and leave comments like a teammate would.
And the Copilot coding agent goes further. Assign it
an issue, and it works in the background —

writing code, running tests in its Actions-powered
environment —
then opens a pull request for you to review.
There's a free tier to start, and paid plans
for heavier use.
You stay the reviewer. The agent does the legwork.
Security is built in, too.

Dependabot watches your dependencies. It raises
alerts for known

vulnerabilities, and opens pull requests that
upgrade them.

Code scanning, powered by CodeQL, analyses your code
for
bugs like injection, and flags them right in the
pull request.

Secret scanning finds leaked keys and tokens. With
push

protection, it blocks the push before the secret
ever
reaches GitHub.
For public repositories, much of this is free. For

private ones, it's sold as GitHub Secret Protection
and
Code Security.
A few more worth knowing.
Releases package versioned downloads with notes.

Packages and the container registry host your images
and
libraries next to the code.

Pages serves free static websites straight from a
repository.
The GitHub CLI, gh, drives pull requests, issues and
workflow runs from your terminal.
Gists share snippets instantly.
Apps from the Marketplace extend GitHub itself.

And Insights shows contributors, traffic, and your
dependency graph.
Let's recap.
Everything is a chain: an event starts a workflow,
a workflow runs jobs, and each job runs steps
on a runner.

Workflows are YAML files in dot github slash
workflows.

Filters decide when they run. needs and matrix
decide
how jobs fan out.

Actions and reusable workflows mean you rarely start
from
scratch.
Caches, outputs and artifacts carry data through.

Environments, approvals and OIDC make deploys safe,
and least
privilege keeps them secure.
And around it all, GitHub gives you pull requests,

issues, projects, Codespaces, Copilot and built-in
security.

Now open a repository, create dot github slash
workflows,
and write your first fifteen lines. Push code. Let
the robots do the rest. Thanks for watching.
